functional.text: Deliver notifications by mobile push (iOS/Android), SMS and email.
Internal services send a notification to a user from a template + params, now or scheduled; campaigns target a segment.
Users opt out per category and channel; marketing is capped at a few per user per day; suppressed sends are recorded.
Producers can look up the status of a notification (queued, sent, failed, suppressed) for 30 days.

non_functional.text: Accepted notifications are never lost (at-least-once to the provider); duplicates suppressed by idempotency key.
Transactional messages (OTP, password reset) handed to the provider within ~5 s p99, even during campaigns; marketing may lag minutes.
One slow or failing provider must not affect the other channels.

assumptions.text: 500M notifications/day (400M push, 80M email, 20M SMS); campaign bursts ×10.
300M devices; ~500 B per log record; ~250 B per device row.

out_of_scope.text: Template authoring UI, audience segmentation engine, in-app inbox.

api.request: user_id | segment_id, template, params, category, priority, channels?, idempotency_key, send_at?
api.notes: Returns after persisting; delivery is asynchronous.
Plus POST /users/{id}/devices {platform, push_token} from the app.

data.name: devices + contacts
data.fields: devices(user_id, device_id, platform, push_token, updated_at); contacts(user_id, email, phone)
data.why: ~75 GB, relational, cached on the hot path.

data.name: preferences
data.why: Read on every send (through a cache), written rarely.

data.name: notification_log
data.fields: notification_id, idempotency_key, user_id, channel, priority, status (queued|sent|failed|suppressed), attempts, provider_msg_id, ts; TTL 30 days
data.why: ~6k writes/s average with bursts, simple key lookups, TTL expiry: ~7.5 TB.

parts.title: Accept fast and enforce policy at one gate
parts.problem: Dozens of teams call the platform (~6k/s average, ~58k/s in campaigns). Each request must be validated, checked against opt-outs and caps, made durable and answered in milliseconds, without waiting on Apple or the SMS vendor, and a retried request must not send twice.

options.name: Synchronous send: call the provider inside the request
options.cons: callers wait seconds on providers; a provider blip loses the message or fails the caller

options.name: Accept, enqueue, and let each channel worker check preferences
options.cons: every worker re-implements policy; one forgotten check sends marketing to an opted-out user

options.name: Accept → check prefs and caps once → write the log (unique idempotency key) → enqueue → 202
options.pros: callers decoupled; policy enforced in exactly one place; the log answers status and dedups retries
options.cons: an extra write per request; the cache must be invalidated when a user opts out

parts.choice: A load-balanced Notification API that checks preferences (cached) and per-user caps, records the request in notification_log under a unique idempotency key, enqueues it and returns 202
parts.why: F3 says no path may skip opt-outs, so the check lives at the only entrance. Providers take seconds and fail, so N1 is met by persisting before acking and delivering later. 300M devices ≈ 75 GB fits a cache, so the check is cheap.

nodes.label: Counters: user caps + provider token buckets

parts.title: Traffic isolation and campaign pacing
parts.problem: A 50M-user campaign and a login code arrive in the same second. The login code must reach its provider within ~5 s, and a slow SMS vendor must not delay push.

options.name: One shared queue
options.cons: the code waits behind 50M marketing messages; a slow SMS vendor blocks push

options.name: Queues per channel
options.pros: a slow vendor only backs up its own channel (N3)
options.cons: inside a channel, codes still wait behind marketing (breaks N2)

options.name: One queue with priority ordering
options.cons: priority queues starve or reorder badly under huge backlogs; most brokers don't do it well

options.name: Queues per channel × priority, dedicated worker pools, and a scheduler that releases campaigns at a set rate
options.pros: N2 and N3 both hold; campaign load is shaped, not dumped
options.cons: more queues and pools to run and size

parts.choice: Separate transactional and bulk queues per channel with their own workers; campaigns enter through a paced scheduler
parts.why: Bulkheads: transactional traffic is small (a few % of volume), so its queues are always near empty and its workers idle-ready. The scheduler turns a 10× burst into a steady flow that providers accept.

parts.title: Provider delivery under limits and failures
parts.problem: Third-party providers throttle (429s), time out and go down for minutes, and SMS costs money. Workers must send at the rate each provider allows, retry without hammering it, never send the same SMS twice, and record the outcome.

options.name: Send as fast as possible, retry immediately on error
options.cons: 429 storms; a sick provider gets hammered; duplicates after ambiguous timeouts

options.name: Buy a single aggregator (CPaaS) and let it handle everything
options.cons: one vendor's outage is your outage; costs more per message; still need idempotency on your side

options.name: Per-provider token buckets + circuit breaker + delay queue with exponential backoff → DLQ, idempotency checked in the log
options.pros: smooth sending under limits; outages wait instead of fail; duplicates prevented
options.cons: shared counter store; more moving parts

parts.choice: Workers take a token from the provider's bucket before each send, send with an idempotency key, and on failure park the message in a delay queue with exponential backoff and jitter; after N tries it goes to a dead-letter queue. Every outcome is written to the log.
parts.why: N1 means at-least-once, and providers fail often, so retries are normal, not exceptional. Token buckets turn 58k/s bursts into what each provider accepts; the log plus provider-side keys make a redelivered message a no-op.

nodes.label: Counters: user caps + provider token buckets

deep_dives.title: Ambiguous timeouts, retries and duplicates

options.name: no retry
options.cons: provider blips lose login codes (breaks N1)

options.name: immediate retry loop in the worker
options.cons: hammers a struggling provider and blocks the worker

options.name: delay queue with exponential backoff + DLQ, idempotency key per (notification, channel)
options.pros: survives outages, bounded load, no double sends

deep_dives.choice: delay queue with exponential backoff + jitter, then a dead-letter queue; idempotency key per (notification, channel) checked in the log and passed to providers that accept one
deep_dives.why: A timeout does not tell you whether the SMS went out. The worker records 'sending' before the call and 'sent' after; a redelivered message that finds 'sent' is skipped, and providers that accept a key dedup the rest. Login codes carry a TTL and are dropped once expired instead of arriving late.

deep_dives.title: Where user caps and provider limits are enforced

options.name: let providers reject excess
options.cons: 429s become retries; user caps are never enforced

options.name: per-user frequency cap in the API + per-provider token buckets in workers
options.pros: users protected once at the gate; provider limits respected smoothly
options.cons: a shared counter store on the hot path

deep_dives.choice: per-user frequency cap checked in the API, per-provider token buckets in the workers, both as Redis counters
deep_dives.why: Caps are a product rule about the user, so they belong at the single gate (P1). Send rates are an operational limit of each provider, so they belong where sending happens (P3); a burst is spread out instead of rejected.

deep_dives.title: Expanding a campaign segment

options.name: API expands the segment into 50M jobs at once
options.cons: 50M enqueues in seconds floods queues and the log

options.name: scheduler pages through the segment and releases batches at a target rate
options.pros: steady load; easy to pause or cancel
options.cons: a campaign takes longer to finish

deep_dives.choice: the scheduler pages through the segment and releases batches at a configured rate per channel
deep_dives.why: Marketing may lag minutes (N2), so trading speed for a smooth load is free; it also makes cancelling a bad campaign possible halfway.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Campaign fan-out from segment to users (scheduler pages through the segment at a set rate), the preferences lookup per send (cache), provider throughput (token buckets, multiple vendors for SMS/email).
wrapup.failures: Provider outage: messages stay queued, backoff + circuit breaker, failover to a secondary SMS/email vendor. Worker crash mid-send: message redelivered, idempotency check prevents a duplicate. Expired OTPs dropped. Poison messages go to the DLQ.
wrapup.monitoring: Queue depth and oldest-message age per channel × priority, accept → sent latency (p99 for transactional), provider error and throttle rates, DLQ size, suppression rate, SMS spend per day.
wrapup.scale: 10×: add queue partitions and workers per channel, shard the log, more vendors for SMS/email, regional deployments near providers.
wrapup.future: Delivery/open tracking via provider webhooks, smart send-time, digesting (batch several notifications into one), in-app inbox.
